summary: Reports on an online workshop run by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) in December 2022 about the environmental costs and benefits of Internet applications and systems. It records discussions of impacts and industry needs, and points to areas for improvement and future work. It is a workshop report, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: People who help design the Internet met online to talk about how it affects nature, like electricity use. This is their written report of what they discussed and what to do next.

subtitle: What the Internet Architecture Board learned about designing networks for environmental sustainability.

tldr.problem: Internet infrastructure and applications consume energy and raw materials, but the technical community lacked a shared understanding of the environmental impacts and did not have clear guidance on how to reduce them responsibly.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board held an online workshop in December 2022 where 73 experts from industry, research, and standards organizations discussed environmental impacts, shared measurements, explored improvements, and identified areas for IETF standards work.
tldr.outcome: The workshop revealed that the problem is complex with no single solution, but identified practical improvements in measurement, protocol efficiency, energy proportionality, and the role of the Internet in enabling less harmful activities. The IAB established an e-impact program for ongoing work.

today: RFC 9547 is an Informational document reporting on an IAB workshop. It does not set technical standards but documents consensus findings and identified research areas. The IAB e-impact program continues this work, and various IETF working groups are pursuing specific improvements in areas like metrics, Time-Variant Routing, and sustainability considerations.

sections.title: The Big Picture: Internet Impact on the Environment
sections.content:
The Internet has environmental costs and benefits. On one hand, it enables virtual meetings and services that reduce the need for physical travel and goods production. On the other hand, Internet systems require energy to operate and raw materials to manufacture, and operate around the clock in data centers and networks worldwide.

The workshop participants emphasized that the environmental impact of the Internet is not just about energy consumption but also about carbon intensity (the emissions per unit of energy), resource extraction, life cycle impacts, and the ways the Internet enables or prevents broader societal resource use. No single improvement will solve the problem, but continuous incremental changes across many areas can add up to significant reductions over time.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet helps us avoid travel and waste, but it also uses a lot of electricity. We need to understand both sides and find ways to make it cleaner.

sections.title: Understanding and Measuring Environmental Impact
sections.content:
A major theme of the workshop was that you cannot improve what you do not measure. Participants discussed the energy consumption of networks, data centers, and user devices, noting that user devices (phones, laptops) often dominate the impact. They also noted that media reports on the Internet's environmental impact often contain significant errors or exaggeration, emphasizing the importance of accurate measurement and data.

Key observations included that some systems lack energy proportionality—they consume nearly the same energy whether running at full capacity or idle. This means that oversizing systems for peak demand results in wasted energy during low-demand periods. Load shifting and better resource utilization could reduce peaks and improve efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can fix the problem, you need to measure it. Many people guess wrong about how much energy the Internet uses, so real data matters.

sections.title: Potential Improvements in Protocol Design
sections.content:
The workshop identified several areas where IETF standards work could improve environmental efficiency. Using efficient binary data formats instead of textual ones (like JSON or XML) can reduce data size and energy consumption when systems are energy-proportional. Examples include CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) and HTTP/2's binary framing.

Multicast was discussed as potentially improving efficiency in some scenarios (such as media distribution), though it faces deployment barriers and may increase overhead in wireless networks. The workshop also noted the importance of designing systems with energy awareness in mind—for instance, allowing devices to sleep or slow down when appropriate, and carrying information about energy availability and carbon intensity so applications can adapt.
sections.plainLanguage: Using simpler, shorter messages costs less energy. Doing more work at night when solar power is available, or when the grid is cleaner, also helps.

sections.title: Actions and Future Work
sections.content:
The workshop identified several actionable areas for the IETF: measurement mechanisms and telemetry to track energy consumption and carbon emissions; protocol design improvements for efficiency; research on the environmental impact of Internet technologies; and awareness within the technical community of sustainability considerations.

The IAB created the e-impact program as a venue for continued discussion and coordination with other standards organizations. Near-term focus areas include improving energy proportionality, using efficient data formats, developing standardized metrics, and avoiding crypto assets where alternatives suffice. Longer-term research includes understanding the impact of business models (like advertising), exploring carbon-aware networking, and optimizing for intermittent connectivity in remote systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet community needs to keep talking about this, measure progress, and try new ideas. Some improvements can happen quickly; others will take years.

sections.title: Scope, Trade-offs, and Responsibilities
sections.content:
The workshop emphasized that reducing the Internet's environmental impact must be done holistically. A local optimization that reduces energy in one part of the network but increases latency or jitter elsewhere might harm the overall system or make virtual meetings less effective, pushing users back to physical travel with greater environmental cost.

The technical community's responsibility is to understand the impacts of its choices, design for efficiency and environmental awareness, and collaborate with other SDOs and industries. However, the workshop acknowledged that not everything is within the technical community's scope: business models, regulatory policy, energy sources, and social factors also shape the Internet's impact.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes trying to save energy in one place makes something else worse. The whole system matters, not just individual parts.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The workshop noted that environmental improvements can have security implications. For example, systems that make energy consumption information available might be tampered with to report false data. Systems that allow control of network elements for optimization purposes could be misused for attacks. The workshop also recommended avoiding crypto assets (such as NFTs and cryptocurrencies) where other mechanisms would suffice, due to their high energy consumption and limited technical benefit.

On the positive side, some environmental improvements align with privacy and security: using less data means less information shared, and designing systems for energy-constrained situations often yields more secure and private systems as a side effect.
sections.plainLanguage: Being greener can also be more secure: if you send less data, fewer people can intercept it. But we have to be careful that systems that measure energy use are not hacked.
